answer:
The original data have  
\[
n=5,\quad \bar x=3,\quad \bar y=4,\quad S_{xx}=10,\quad S_{xy}=15.
\]

Adding the point \((9,4)\), the new sample size is \(6\):
\[
\bar x_{\text{new}}=\frac{5(3)+9}{6}=4,
\qquad
\bar y_{\text{new}}=\frac{5(4)+4}{6}=4.
\]

Update the corrected sums:

For \(x\),
\[
S_{xx,\text{new}}=10+\frac{5\cdot 1}{6}(9-3)^2
=10+\frac{5}{6}(36)=40.
\]

For the cross-product, since the added point has \(y=4\), equal to the original mean \(\bar y=4\),
\[
S_{xy,\text{new}}=15.
\]

Therefore the new least-squares slope is
\[
b=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac{15}{40}=\frac38.
\]
The new intercept is
\[
a=\bar y_{\text{new}}-b\bar x_{\text{new}}
=4-\frac38(4)
=4-\frac32
=\frac52.
\]

So the new fitted regression line is
\[
\boxed{\hat y=\frac52+\frac38 x}
\]
or
\[
\boxed{\hat y=2.5+0.375x}.
\]

Check the new mean point \((4,4)\):
\[
\hat y=\frac52+\frac38(4)
=\frac52+\frac32
=4.
\]
Thus the fitted line does pass through the new mean point
\[
\boxed{(4,4)}.
\]

Final answers:
\[
\boxed{\text{slope }=\frac38=0.375,\qquad \text{intercept }=\frac52=2.5.}
\]
The line is \(\boxed{\hat y=2.5+0.375x}\), and it passes through \((\bar x,\bar y)=(4,4)\).
